docs.title: Several derived columns, and the design
docs.text:
Each recipe reads one sheet and writes another, so to add several columns, run them one after another, each reading the sheet the one before wrote. Then name the derived column in the design, as any other column:

$ detk-de deseq2 -o de_results.csv "counts ~ age_zscore + condition[control]" counts.csv sample_info.age_zscore.csv

Each detk-util record wrote a module JSON document to detk_report/json/ naming the tool, mlr, and its version, with the command and the checksum of every file it read and wrote. So detk-report generate lists each recipe as a recorded step, and the provenance crate shows it as the step that produced the sheet detk-de read (see detk-util record).

docs.title: Tools overview
docs.text:
detk is organized into modules, each exposed both as a subcommand of detk and as a standalone executable (detk stats ... ≡ detk-stats ...):

Tool Purpose Needs R detk-stats count matrix statistics (distributions, zeros, entropy, PCA) no detk-filter filter features with a mini-language no detk-norm DESeq2 / library-size / FPKM normalization no detk-transform plog / rlog / VST transformations rlog, vst detk-de DESeq2 and Firth logistic differential expression yes detk-enrich fgsea pre-ranked gene set enrichment yes detk-outlier outlier count identification and shrinkage no detk-util tidy counts/column-data files against each other no detk-wrapr run custom R scripts through the detk R bridge yes detk-report render accumulated results into an HTML report no

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
Every subcommand accepts these options in addition to its own:

Common options:
    -d CHAR --out-delim=CHAR  Delimiter to use for output file [default: ,]
    --report-dir=DIR          Specify the report directory [default: ./detk_report]
    --no-report               Do not generate the HTML report
    --version                 Print out detk version and exit
    -v --verbose              Make log output verbose
    -q --quiet                Turn off all logging except warnings and errors
    --shut-up                 Turn off ALL logging

Most tools write their primary output to stdout by default and accept -o FILE/--output=FILE to write to a file instead. Unless --no-report is given, each invocation also records a JSON document under <report-dir>/json/ for the report.

docs.title: de — differential expression
docs.text:
Important

The model formulas in this module use detk's formula mini-language. Read that first before writing your models.

Also remember to filter prior to differential expression — the number of genes provided for hypothesis testing affects the results. You may need to filter out genes with zero expression in all samples of interest.

Each method accepts a design formula, a counts matrix file, and a column data file. Both methods run in R via the wrapr bridge and require the corresponding R package.

docs.title: deseq2
docs.text:
Command line interface to a canonical DESeq2 analysis:

detk-de deseq2 "counts ~ AgeOfDeath + Status" raw_counts.csv column_data.csv > deseq2_results.csv

Tip

  • You can provide the whole raw counts matrix with a column data file containing only the samples you care about — detk subsets for you.
  • Add brackets with the name of the reference group to control what you are comparing against, e.g. "counts ~ Status[control]".

This is roughly equivalent to the following R:

library(DESeq2)

counts <- read.csv("raw_counts.csv", rownames=1)
design.mat <- read.csv("column_data.csv")

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData = counts,
    colData = design.mat,
    design = ~ AgeOfDeath + Status
)

dds <- DESeq(dds, minReplicatesForReplace=Inf)
write.csv(results(dds, cooksCutoff=Inf), de.out.fn)

The analysis implemented here differs from the default DESeq2 analysis in the following ways:

  • the design formula must have counts as the only term on the left hand side
  • no outlier mean trimming based on Cook's distance is performed
  • no p-values or adjusted p-values are flagged or omitted due to outliers
  • estimated parameters, statistics, and p-values are reported for all variables in the model, rather than just the last term (request the DESeq2 default with --last-term-only)
  • no independent filtering is performed
  • every output column is prefixed with its model term, e.g. Status__log2FoldChange
Usage:
    detk-de deseq2 [options] <design> <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of primary output [default: stdout]
    --rda=RDA              Filename passed to saveRDS() R function of the result
                           objects from the analysis
    --strict               Require that the sample order indicated by the column names in the
                           counts file are the same as, and in the same order as, the
                           sample order in the row names of the covariates file
    --norm-counts          Prevent DESeq2 from normalizing counts prior to
                           running differential expression, default behavior
                           assumes that provided counts are raw
    --last-term-only       Use the default DESeq2 behavior of returning DE parameters
                           for the last term in the model, default behavior is to
                           report parameters for all variables in the model
    --gene-wise-disp       Use estimateDispersionsGeneEst instead of estimateDispersions
    --cores=N              Tell DESeq2 to use N cores when running, requires the
                           BiocParallel Bioconductor package to be installed [default: none]

docs.title: firth
docs.text:
When comparing two classes of samples, Firth's logistic regression as described by Choi et al has desirable statistical properties: a better controlled type I error rate, and less loss of power from including additional covariates, compared with other DE methods including DESeq2. It uses a penalized likelihood to avoid complete separation of the data, a common occurrence in RNA-seq. The trade-off is that it needs more samples than negative-binomial methods — at least ~10 replicates per condition.

A counts term must be included on the right hand side of the design formula, with the sample class on the left:

detk-de firth "Status ~ AgeOfDeath + counts" norm_counts.csv column_data.csv > firth_results.csv

Usage:
    detk-de firth [options] <design> <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of primary output [default: stdout]
    --rda=RDA              Filename passed to saveRDS() R function of the result
                           objects from the analysis
    --strict               Require that the sample order indicated by the column names in the
                           counts file are the same as, and in the same order as, the
                           sample order in the row names of the covariates file
    --standardize          Standardize counts prior to running logistic regression
                           as to obtain standardized (i.e. directly comparable)
                           beta coefficients
    --cores=N              Tell R to use N cores when running, requires the
                           parallel R package to be installed [default: none]

docs.title: enrich — set enrichment methods
docs.text: Statistical set enrichment methods, currently pre-ranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis via the fgsea Bioconductor package (requires R).

docs.title: fgsea
docs.text:
Perform pre-ranked GSEA on a differential expression (or any) result file against a GMT gene set file.

The GMT file must be tab delimited with the set name in the first column, a description in the second (ignored by detk), and one feature ID per column after that — one feature set per line. The result file can be any character delimited file with column names in the first row.

The feature IDs must come from the same identifier system (gene symbols, ENSGIDs, ...) in both files. You will likely need to provide:

  • -i <col> — column in the results file containing feature IDs
  • -c <col> — column containing the ranking statistic, e.g. cond__log2FoldChange
detk-enrich fgsea -o gsea_results.csv -i gene -c cond__log2FoldChange msigdb_c2cp.gmt deseq2_results.csv

Usage:
    detk-enrich fgsea [options] <gmt_fn> <result_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE     Destination of fgsea output [default: stdout]
    -p PROCS --cores=PROCS    Ask BiocParallel to use PROCS processes when
                              executing fgsea in parallel, requires the
                              BiocParallel package to be installed
    -i FIELD --idcol=FIELD    Column name or 0-based integer index to use as
                              the gene identifier [default: 0]
    -c FIELD --statcol=FIELD  Column name or 0-based integer index to use as
                              the statistic for ranking, defaults to the last
                              numeric column in the file
    -a --ascending            Sort column ascending, default is to sort
                              descending, use this if you are sorting by p-value
                              or want to reverse the directionality of the NES
                              scores
    --abs                     Take the absolute value of the column before
                              passing to fgsea
    --filter-unannotated      Remove any genes from the result matrix that have
                              identifiers that don't exist in any gene set of
                              the GMT
    --minSize=INT             minSize argument to fgsea [default: 15]
    --maxSize=INT             maxSize argument to fgsea [default: 500]
    --nperm=INT               nperm argument to fgsea [default: 10000]
    --multilevel              Use the fgseaMultilevel function, instead of fgsea
    --rda=FILE                write out the fgsea result to the provide file
                              using saveRDS() in R

docs.title: filter — filtering count matrices
docs.text:
Filter features (rows) out of a counts matrix using a compact filter mini-language.

Usage:
    detk-filter [options] <command> <counts_fn> [<cov_fn>]

Options:
    -o <out_fn> --output=<out_fn>    Name of output file [default: stdout]

Quick start — keep only genes with a mean count greater than 10:

detk-filter -o counts_gt10.csv 'mean(all) > 10' norm_counts.csv

docs.title: The filter mini-language
docs.text:
A filter command has the form, enclosed in single or double quotes:

<function>(<column spec>) <inequality> <number>

The command describes rows that should be kept; rows not meeting the criterion are filtered out.

Available filter functions:

Function Keeps rows based on... mean the mean value across the column spec median the median value across the column spec max the maximum value across the column spec min the minimum value across the column spec zero how many counts are zero. A number strictly between 0 and 1 is interpreted as a fraction of samples; 0 or ≥ 1 as an absolute number of samples nonzero how many counts are nonzero, with the same fraction/absolute interpretation

The supported inequalities are >, >=, <, <=, ==, and !=. Numbers may be positive or negative, integer or floating point. Whitespace is ignored: mean(all)>10 ≡ mean(all) > 10.

Terms combine with and / or. and binds tighter than or, and both group to the left, as in Python, SQL and R. So

mean(all) > 5 and nonzero(all) > 0.9 or mean(all) > 100

is read as (mean(all) > 5 and nonzero(all) > 0.9) or mean(all) > 100, and a or b and c as a or (b and c). Parentheses group as written:

mean(all) > 10 and zero(all) < 0.5
(mean(all) > 5 and nonzero(all) > 0.9) or mean(all) > 100

The second example keeps lowly-but-consistently expressed rows plus any row with an overall mean above 100.

docs.title: Incorporating column data
docs.text:
Passing a column data file lets filters operate per sample group. Given column data like:

sample_name, condition
A, test
B, test
C, test
D, control
E, control

Group-wise filtering — name a column data column as the column spec, and the filter is applied to each group separately; a row is kept if any group passes:

mean(condition) > 10

keeps genes whose mean count exceeds 10 in either the test or control samples. This enables expressive schemes like:

nonzero(condition) > 0.5

which retains genes expressed in more than half the samples of either condition — genes uniquely expressed in one group survive, where filtering on the overall mean would discard them.

Group-specific filtering — subset to one level of the column:

mean(condition[test]) > 10

keeps genes whose mean exceeds 10 in the test samples, regardless of the control counts.

docs.title: norm — normalizing count matrices
docs.text: Count normalization strategies. None of these subcommands require R — the DESeq2 procedure is a Python port.

docs.title: deseq2
docs.text:
Normalize using the median-of-ratios method as implemented in the R package DESeq2: each sample is divided by a size factor calculated as the median ratio of each gene count to the geometric mean count across all samples.

Usage:
    detk-norm deseq2 [options] <counts_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE        Destination of normalized output in CSV format [default: stdout]
    --size-factors=FILE          Write out the size factors found by the DESeq2
                                 method to two column tab separated file where
                                 the first column is sample name and the second
                                 column is the size factor

The implementation is roughly equivalent to the following R:

library(DESeq2)

counts <- as.matrix(read.table(counts.fn, row.names=1))
colData <- data.frame(name=seq(ncol(counts)))

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData=counts,
    colData=colData,
    design = ~ 1
)

dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds)
write.table(counts(dds, normalized=TRUE), norm.counts.fn)

docs.title: library
docs.text:
Library size normalization: counts in each column are divided by the sum of that column, so each column of the output sums to 1. Use cpm for the same values scaled to counts per million.

Usage:
    detk-norm library [options] <counts_fn>

docs.title: cpm
docs.text:
Counts Per Million: counts in each column are divided by the sum of that column and multiplied by one million, so each column of the output sums to 1,000,000. This is library scaled by 10^6. A sample with zero total counts produces NaN values and a warning.

Usage:
    detk-norm cpm [options] <counts_fn>

docs.title: fpkm
docs.text:
Fragments Per Kilobase per Million reads: each count is divided by the feature's length in kilobases, then by the sample's library size (the total of its column of counts) in millions:

FPKM[g, s] = count[g, s] / (length[g] / 1000) / (library_size[s] / 10^6)
           = count[g, s] * 10^9 / (length[g] * library_size[s])
library_size[s] = sum over g of count[g, s]

For example, a feature 2,000 bases long with 3 counts, in a sample whose counts total 4, has FPKM 3 × 10^9 / (2000 × 4) = 375,000. FPKM is CPM divided by the length in kilobases. A sample whose counts are all zero has no FPKM values: its column is empty (NaN) and a warning is logged.

Changed in 1.0

Before 1.0 (0.9.x), fpkm computed count / (10^6 × length), without dividing by library size. Values from 1.0 on differ from 0.9.x output and are the documented FPKM.

detk must be given the length of every feature in the counts file, as a two-column character-delimited file (format is sniffed) of feature identifier and length in bases:

  • every feature in the counts file must have an entry in the lengths file
  • every length must be a positive number; a zero, negative, missing or non-numeric length is refused (reported as not a positive number)
  • each feature may be listed only once; a lengths file that lists a feature twice is refused
  • the lengths file may contain unused entries
  • the two files do not need to be in the same order
  • feature identifiers are read and matched as text, exactly as written: numeric identifiers (such as Entrez gene IDs) match, a zero-padded 007 matches only 007 (not 7), and every identifier appears in the output as in the counts file
  • an optional header line is allowed: the first line is skipped as a header only when its length field is text that is neither a number nor a missing-value token (empty, NA, NaN, N/A, NULL, None); otherwise it is read as a feature
Usage:
    detk-norm fpkm [options] <counts_fn> <lengths_fn>

docs.title: tpm
docs.text:
Transcripts Per Million: each count is divided by the feature's length in kilobases, giving a per-kilobase rate, and each column of rates is then scaled to sum to 1,000,000:

rate[g, s] = count[g, s] / (length[g] / 1000)
TPM[g, s]  = rate[g, s] / sum over g of rate[g, s] * 10^6

Unlike FPKM, TPM values sum to the same total in every sample, so the proportion of a sample's transcripts a feature represents is comparable across samples. When every feature has the same length, TPM equals CPM.

tpm takes the same lengths file as fpkm, with the same rules (including the optional header line and the refusal of duplicated feature identifiers, and the requirement that every length be a positive number). The output has the same rows, in the same order, as the counts file. A sample whose counts are all zero has no TPM (or CPM) values: its column is empty (NaN) and a warning is logged.

Usage:
    detk-norm tpm [options] <counts_fn> <lengths_fn>

docs.title: outlier — outlier identification
docs.text: Functions for identifying and manipulating outlier counts.

docs.title: entropy
docs.text:
Identify samples that dominate low-entropy features. See detk-stats entropy for the underlying statistic.

Usage:
    detk-outlier entropy <counts_fn> [options]

Options:
    -p P --percentile=P    Float value between 0 and 1
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Name of the output csv
    --plot-output=FILE     Name of the plot png

docs.title: shrink
docs.text:
Iteratively shrink counts that contribute an outsized fraction of a feature's mass toward the feature's distribution, using a probability-mass-function transform.

Usage:
    detk-outlier shrink [options] <counts_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE   Destination of primary output [default: stdout]
    -f N --shrink-factor=N  Shrinkage factor number float between 0 and 1 [default: 0.25]
    -p N --p-max=N          Percent counts of sample default is sqrt(1/num samples)
    -i N --iters=N          Number of iterations [default: 1000]

docs.title: stats — count matrix statistics
docs.text:
Easy access to informative count matrix statistics. Each subcommand produces:

  • a tabular form of the statistics on stdout (or -o FILE), formatted as CSV or a human-readable table (-f table, via terminaltables)
  • a JSON document recorded under the report directory with the same statistics in machine-parsable form

docs.title: Tabular output format
docs.text:
Each tool prints CSV to standard output by default:

$ detk-stats basestats test_counts.csv
stat,val
num_cols,3
num_rows,4

Pass -f table to pretty-print instead:

$ detk-stats basestats -f table test_counts.csv
+basestats-+-----+
| stat     | val |
+----------+-----+
| num_cols | 4   |
| num_rows | 3   |
+----------+-----+

The summary subcommand runs multiple subtools; its CSV output separates each tool's table with a #<name> comment line, and its pretty-printed output prints each table serially.

docs.title: summary
docs.text:
Run the whole stats battery at once — equivalent to running basestats, coldist, colzero, rowzero, entropy, and pca separately.

Usage:
    detk-stats summary [options] <counts_fn> [<cov_fn>]

Options:
    --color-col=COLNAME    Use column data column COLNAME for coloring output plots
    --bins=BINS            Number of bins to use for the calculated
                           distributions [default: 20]
    --log                  log transform count statistics
    --density              Produce density distribution by dividing each distribution
                           by the appropriate sum
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of primary output [default: stdout]
    -f FMT --format=FMT    Format of output, either csv or table [default: csv]

docs.title: basestats
docs.text:
Basic statistics of the counts file: number of samples and number of rows.

Usage:
    detk-stats basestats [options] <counts_fn>

docs.title: coldist
docs.text:
Column-wise distribution of counts. Each column is binned by percentile, with output identical to that produced by np.histogram. Recorded per column: the bin boundaries, the (raw or density) mass in each bin, and extrema beyond 1.5× the inner quartile range.

Usage:
    detk-stats coldist [options] <counts_fn>

Options:
    --bins=N               The number of bins to use when computing the counts
                           distribution [default: 20]
    --log                  Perform a log10 transform on the counts before
                           calculating the distribution. Zeros are omitted
                           prior to histogram calculation.
    --density              Return a density distribution instead of counts,
                           such that the sum of values in *dist* for each
                           column approximately sum to 1.

docs.title: rowdist
docs.text:
Row-wise analog of coldist: the distribution of counts within each feature across samples.

Usage:
    detk-stats rowdist [options] <counts_fn>

Options:
    --bins=N               The number of bins to use when computing the counts
                           distribution [default: 20]
    --log                  Perform a log10 transform on the counts before
                           calculating the distribution
    --density              Return a density distribution instead of counts

docs.title: colzero
docs.text:
Number and fraction of exact-zero counts for each column (sample), along with the column mean and the mean of only the non-zero counts.

Usage:
    detk-stats colzero [options] <counts_fn>

docs.title: rowzero
docs.text:
Number and fraction of exact-zero counts for each row (feature) — the key statistic for deciding filtering thresholds.

Usage:
    detk-stats rowzero [options] <counts_fn>

docs.title: entropy
docs.text:
Row-wise Shannon entropy of counts across samples. For each row, the fraction of the row's counts contributed by each sample is treated as a probability distribution and its entropy H = -Σ p_i · log2(p_i) computed. Rows with very low H have most of their count mass in a small number of samples — these are the rows likely to drive spurious results in downstream analysis, e.g. differential expression.

Usage:
    detk-stats [options] entropy <counts_fn>

docs.title: pca
docs.text:
Principal component analysis of the counts matrix, returning component weights, scores, and variances. Supplying a column data file annotates each sample's projection with covariate values so that sample groups can be distinguished in the report's PCA plot.

Usage:
    detk-stats pca [options] <counts_fn> [<cov_fn>]

docs.title: transform — count transformations
docs.text: Transformations of the distribution of counts in a matrix. plog is pure Python; rlog and vst wrap DESeq2 in R.

docs.title: plog
docs.text:
Pseudo-log transform: log(counts + pseudocount).

Usage:
    detk-transform plog [options] <counts_fn>

Options:
    -c N --pseudocount=N   The pseudocount to use when taking the log transform [default: 1]
    -b B --base=B          The base of the log to use [default: 10]
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of primary output [default: stdout]

docs.title: rlog
docs.text:
Command line interface to the DESeq2 regularized-log transformation. As in the originating package, the default is a blind transformation, i.e. without respect to an experimental design:

detk-transform rlog norm_counts.csv > rlog_norm_counts.csv

To perform a non-blind transformation, provide a design formula and column data file:

detk-transform rlog norm_counts.csv "counts ~ AgeOfDeath + Status" column_data.csv > rlog_nonblind.csv

Usage:
    detk-transform rlog [options] <counts_fn> [<design> <cov_fn>]

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of primary output [default: stdout]
    --rda=RDA              Filename passed to saveRDS() R function of the result
                           objects from the analysis
    --strict               Require that the sample order indicated by the column names in the
                           counts file are the same as, and in the same order as, the
                           sample order in the row names of the covariates file

docs.title: vst
docs.text:
Command line interface to the DESeq2 variance-stabilizing transformation:

detk-transform vst norm_counts.csv > vst_norm_counts.csv

Usage:
    detk-transform vst [options] <counts_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of primary output [default: stdout]
    --rda=RDA              Filename passed to saveRDS() R function of the result
                           objects from the analysis

docs.title: util — counts, column data and result file utilities
docs.text: Functions for tidying up counts and column data files — mostly subsetting one or the other so the sample IDs and their order match. Combined with csvgrep from csvkit, this is useful for extracting subsets of samples for downstream differential expression analysis. gather builds the counts matrix from per-sample quantifier outputs in the first place, and annotate adds feature metadata, such as gene symbols, to a result table. record runs a command outside detk (Miller, awk, an R script) and records it as a step, so the files it writes have a producer in detk's provenance.

docs.title: gather
docs.text:
Combine per-sample outputs of salmon (quant.sf), kallisto (abundance.tsv), htseq-count or featureCounts into one counts matrix, with a row per feature and a column per sample, ready for every other detk tool.

Usage:
    detk-util gather [options] <files>...

Options:
    --format=FMT           salmon, kallisto, htseq, featurecounts or auto
                           [default: auto]
    --column=COL           Column to extract from each file, by name or 0-based
                           position (default: the format's count column)
    --name-from=REGEX      Regular expression deriving each sample name from
                           its file path (the first group, or the whole match)
    --on-mismatch=WHAT     What to do when the samples list different features:
                           error, fill (with 0) or drop [default: error]
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of the counts matrix [default: stdout]

For a salmon run per sample in sample_1__salmon/, sample_2__salmon/, ...:

detk-util gather --name-from='(sample_[0-9]+)__salmon' -o raw_counts.csv \
    sample_*__salmon/quant.sf

Formats. With --format=auto (the default) each file's format is detected from its first lines, never from its name: salmon and kallisto by their exact header line, featureCounts by its # Program:featureCounts line or its Geneid Chr Start End Strand Length header, and htseq-count by a first line with no header whose fields after the ID are integers. Every file must have the same format; a file that matches none of these is refused with a request for --format.

Columns. One column is extracted from each file, as written:

format default column other useful columns salmon NumReads TPM kallisto est_counts tpm htseq the count column (1) featurecounts every count column one BAM's column

Pick another with --column, by header name or 0-based position. htseq-count 0.13 and later, given several BAM files, writes one count column per BAM and no header naming them; such a file is refused unless --column picks one of its columns (--column=2 for the second BAM), so that no sample is lost silently. Run htseq-count once per sample to gather them all.

Feature IDs and values are kept exactly as written (9.512 stays 9.512, 007 stays 007). Every value must be a plain finite number as quantifiers write them: digits with an optional sign, decimal fraction and exponent (42, 9.512, 1.5e-06). Anything else, including NA, nan, inf, padded values and digit separators (1_000, 1,000), is an error, as is a feature listed twice in one file. htseq-count's summary lines (__no_feature, __ambiguous, ...) are not features: they are left out of the matrix and their values recorded in the report. gather does no aggregation: transcript-level salmon or kallisto output gives a transcript-level matrix.

Sample names. By default a sample is named after its file, without the last extension (s1.counts.txt becomes s1.counts). When those names are not unique among the files given, as with salmon's quant.sf and kallisto's abundance.tsv, every sample is named after the directory holding its file instead, all or nothing. A default name therefore depends on the other files in the run: a single s1/quant.sf is named quant, but s1 when gathered with s2/quant.sf. Use --name-from for names that never change. With --name-from, the name is the first group of the regular expression, or else its whole match, searched in the path as given. In featureCounts output each count column is a sample, named the same way from the column header (the BAM file's path), so bam/A.bam becomes A. Two samples with the same name are an error.

Order. The samples are written in the order of the files on the command line (featureCounts' columns in their order within the file). A quoted glob that gather expands itself is taken in natural order, comparing runs of digits as numbers, so s2 comes before s10; a glob the shell expands is in the shell's order, which is usually s1, s10, s2. detk's other tools match samples by name, so the order rarely matters.

Features. The rows follow the first sample's features. Samples quantified against the same index or annotation list the same features, so by default a difference is an error that says which samples lack how many features, with examples; it usually means a sample was quantified against another annotation. When the difference is expected, --on-mismatch=fill keeps every feature (features some samples lack are appended in order of appearance) and writes 0 where a sample lacks one, and --on-mismatch=drop keeps only the features every sample lists.

The report records the format, the column, the samples and their source files, the number of features, how many features and values were filled or dropped with examples, and htseq-count's summary lines. The input files are listed in the module's parameters (files).

docs.title: tidy
docs.text:
Subset both the counts columns and the column data rows by intersection, returning new outputs for both. The tidied column data is only written if you pass -p.

Usage:
    detk-util tidy [options] <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of tidied counts data [default: stdout]
    -p FILE --column-data-output=FILE  Destination of tidied column data

docs.title: tidy-counts
docs.text:
Subset and order the counts file columns according to the rows of the column data file. Fails if the column data contains samples missing from the counts file.

Usage:
    detk-util tidy-counts [options] <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of tidied counts data [default: stdout]

docs.title: tidy-covs
docs.text:
Subset and order the column data rows according to the columns of the counts file. Fails if the counts file contains samples missing from the column data.

Usage:
    detk-util tidy-covs [options] <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

Options:
    -o FILE --output=FILE  Destination of tidied column data [default: stdout]

docs.title: annotate
docs.text:
Add feature metadata, such as gene symbols, to a result table (for example the output of detk-de) by joining it with a mapping table on the feature IDs. The mapping is a plain delimited file you supply, so the result does not depend on a network service or on when it was run: a BioMart export, a table derived from a GTF, or a dump of a Bioconductor org.*.db package all work.

Usage:
    detk-util annotate [options] <result_fn> <mapping_fn>

Options:
    -i FIELD --idcol=FIELD  Column in the result file holding the feature IDs to
                            join on [default: 0]
    --map-from=COL          Column in the mapping file matching the result IDs
                            [default: 0]
    --map-to=COLS           Comma-separated mapping columns to add, or 'all' for
                            every column but --map-from [default: all]
    --strip-versions        Strip trailing .N version suffixes from Ensembl-style
                            IDs on both sides before joining
    --drop-unmapped         Drop result rows with no mapping instead of leaving
                            their added columns empty
    -o FILE --output=FILE   Destination of the annotated table [default: stdout]

Columns are named by header or by 0-based position. The result table is read and written back as text, so it keeps its rows, their order, its columns and their order, and every value as written, including numeric IDs such as Entrez IDs with leading zeros (007 stays 007 and matches 007 in the mapping). The added columns come after the result's own; with -i naming a column other than the first, that column stays where it was.

  • An ID is mapped when at least one mapping row gives it a non-empty value in one of the added columns. A mapping row whose added columns are all empty is ignored, so with --map-to=hgnc_symbol an ID whose only rows have no symbol is unmapped, even though the mapping lists it.
  • An unmapped ID gets empty added columns, unless --drop-unmapped removes the row.
  • An empty or missing ID (an empty cell, NA, NaN and the other strings pandas reads as missing) is never joined: it counts as unmapped, and the report counts these rows separately.
  • An ID with several mapping rows (one Ensembl gene with two Entrez IDs, say) gets the distinct values of each added column joined with ;.
  • An added column whose name the result table already has is renamed with the suffix _annot.

Version suffixes are the most common reason a join silently finds nothing: ENSG00000141510.17 in the counts does not match ENSG00000141510 in a BioMart export. --strip-versions removes them before joining, and the log warns with example IDs when some features stay unmapped.

detk-util annotate --strip-versions --map-to=hgnc_symbol \
    -o de_results_annotated.csv de_results.csv biomart_export.tsv

The report records how many result rows were mapped, left unmapped, had an empty or missing ID, matched several mapping rows or were dropped (these count rows, so a duplicated ID counts once per row), the columns added and up to ten distinct unmapped IDs.

docs.title: record
docs.text:
Run a command outside detk and record it as a step of the analysis. A step outside detk otherwise leaves a gap in the provenance: a detk-de run would show its column data as a file no step produced. record runs the command and writes a module JSON document for it, so the report lists the step and the provenance crate (ro-crate-metadata.json) shows it as the producer of its outputs, and a later detk command that reads them traces back to it.

Usage:
    detk-util record [options] [-i FILE]... -o FILE... -- <command> [<arg>...]

Options:
    -i FILE --input=FILE   A file the command reads; give it once per file,
                           or not at all
    -o FILE --output=FILE  A file the command writes; give it once per file
                           (at least one)
    --tool=NAME            Name of the tool that runs (default: the base name
                           of the command's first word)
    --tool-version=TEXT    Version of the tool to record (default: the first
                           line of '<command> --version')

Derive an age_group column with Miller and use it in a design:

detk-util record -i sample_info.csv -o sample_info_derived.csv -- \
    mlr --icsv --ocsv put '$age_group = $age >= 50 ? "old" : "young"' \
    sample_info.csv > sample_info_derived.csv
detk-de deseq2 -o de_results.csv "counts ~ age_group" counts.csv sample_info_derived.csv

The command. Everything after -- is the command, run as given, without a shell: words after -- that look like detk's options (-o, --version) are the command's. A pipeline, a redirect inside the step or a glob needs a shell, given explicitly as sh -c '...'; name the tool with --tool then:

detk-util record --tool=awk -i counts.csv -o counts_head.csv -- \
    sh -c 'head -n 101 counts.csv | awk -F, "NF > 1" > counts_head.csv'

The command reads detk's stdin and writes to detk's stdout and stderr, so a redirect of the whole line, as in the Miller example, captures the command's own output; record itself writes nothing to stdout, and its messages go to stderr like every detk command's.

The checks. Every --input must exist before the run (the command does not run otherwise) and every --output after it. record exits 1, with the cause on the last line of stderr, and writes no module JSON when an input is missing, when the command is not found, cannot be run or exits non-zero (whatever its status, record's is 1), or when an output is missing after the run. It never deletes or rewrites a file, so what a failed command wrote is left as it is.

An output that already existed passes the check

The check asks only that each output exists after the run, not that the command wrote it. A file left from an earlier run passes, and so does the file a shell redirect creates: in detk-util record ... -- cmd > out.csv the shell creates out.csv before record starts, so a command that writes nothing still leaves an (empty) out.csv. The checksums the record takes say what each output held after the run; check the file itself when it matters, or delete stale outputs before recording.

The tool and its version. The tool is the base name of the command's first word (mlr), unless --tool names it; give --tool when the first word is a launcher, as with sh -c '...' or Rscript script.R. The version is --tool-version when given; otherwise record runs <first word> --version (with a 10 second timeout, its output captured, not shown) and records the first line it prints. When that fails or prints nothing, or --tool names a tool other than the command's first word, the version is unknown and record warns; that is not an error, since some tools have no --version.

Give --tool-version for your own scripts

When the command is your own script (./derive.py ...), asking it for its version runs ./derive.py --version, and a script that does not handle --version then runs a second time, with whatever it does. Give the version yourself, such as a git commit of the script: --tool-version=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD).

What is recorded. The module JSON document (name record) holds, in its parameters, the command (as one shell-quoted string, and as the list of its words), the tool, its version and the input and output files as given; in its properties, the SHA-256 checksum and size of every input (read before the run) and every output (read after it), and the exit status. Its envelope lists every file in in_file_paths and out_file_paths (schema 1.1), the first of each also being in_file_path and out_file_path. In the crate the step is a CreateAction whose instrument is the tool, with its version, and whose object and result are every input and output, each with its checksum. The HTML report lists the step as "Recorded external step" with its data; it has no chart.

docs.title: wrapr — thin wrapper for running R scripts
docs.text:
Thin wrapper interface for running R scripts from detk. This is a replacement for rpy2, a heavy dependency fraught with danger and hardship.

Note

This module is mostly intended for internal use by detk when interacting with R. A CLI interface is provided because why not, but is only intended for advanced cases where you want to command-line-ize an R script that fits the interface. If you have a one-off R script that needs to be integrated into your workflow, it would probably be better to just run it with R. Caveat emptor.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
wrapr assumes R and any necessary packages are already installed. With conda/mamba:

mamba install -c conda-forge r-base r-jsonlite

The jsonlite R package is required. Verify your environment:

$ detk wrapr check
R found: True
R path: /usr/bin/Rscript
jsonlite found: True

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
wrapr implements a well-defined interface between detk and R through a bridge script. From the command line:

detk-wrapr run \
  --meta-in=/path/to/metadata \        # metadata filename corresponding to input counts
  --meta-out=/path/to/metadata_out \   # where modified metadata should be written
  --params-in=/path/to/params.json \   # JSON file with parameters needed by R
  --params-out=/path/to/params_out.json \  # where R can pass parameters back out
  /path/to/rscript \                   # R script written to use the interface
  /path/to/input_counts \              # counts matrix
  /path/to/output                      # where tabular output should be written

Arguments starting with -- are optional. Input metadata and counts should be tabular as accepted elsewhere by detk. The input parameters file should be JSON containing an object whose fields map directly to R list members.

The bridge script makes the following variables available in the R environment where the script runs:

  • counts.fn — path to the counts file provided to detk-wrapr
  • out.fn — path where new counts should be written after R has operated on them, e.g. write.csv(counts.mat, out.fn)
  • params — an R list containing the values from the parameter JSON file

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Say we want an R script that adds a configurable pseudocount to every count. Write the parameter file:

{
  "pseudocount": 1
}

and the script pseudocount.R:

# counts.fn, params, and out.fn are already defined
mat <- read.csv(counts.fn, rownames=1, colnames=1)
new.mat <- mat + params$pseudocount
write.csv(new.mat, out.fn)

then run:

detk wrapr run --params-in=pseudocount_params.json \
  pseudocount.R counts.csv counts_plus_pseudo.csv

counts_plus_pseudo.csv will contain the result. See the API reference for the WrapR class used internally.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each tutorial is a complete session you can follow at the command line: every command on the page runs in order, from an empty directory, and the outputs the page shows are what you should see. The same pages run as detk's integration tests, so a tutorial that no longer works fails the test suite before it reaches you.

Tutorial What it covers Needs Differential expression on airway statistics, filtering, DESeq2 normalization, VST, outliers, detk-de deseq2, gene symbols, the report and the crate detk, R with DESeq2 and airway From quantifier outputs to a normalized matrix gathering salmon quant.sf files, a sample sheet, CPM and TPM, transforms, statistics and the report detk only Derived covariates and recorded steps deriving covariates with Miller, recording each step with detk-util record, using a derived covariate in a DESeq2 design detk, R with DESeq2 and airway, Miller (mlr)

The tutorials are being written for detk 1.0; each row links to its page once the page is in place.

docs.title: Following a tutorial
docs.text: Start in an empty directory with detk installed (see the quickstart), and run the commands in the order the page shows them. A tutorial that needs R expects Rscript on your PATH with the listed packages installed; one that needs Miller expects mlr.

docs.title: Running a tutorial as a test
docs.text:
From a checkout of the repository, run one tutorial by name:

$ uv run pytest tests/tutorials -k quantifiers

or all of them with uv run pytest tests/tutorials. A tutorial whose requirements (R, an R package, Miller) are missing is skipped, with the reason shown by pytest -rs.

docs.title: Differential expression on airway
docs.text:
This tutorial runs a complete differential expression analysis on a real, public RNA-seq dataset: summary statistics, filtering, DESeq2 normalization, a variance-stabilizing transform, outlier flags, DESeq2's test for the treatment effect with the cell line as a covariate, gene symbols on the results, and the report and provenance crate at the end. The report it makes is detk's published example:

open the finished example report (one self-contained HTML file: everything runs in your browser, nothing is sent anywhere). The run's provenance is published next to it as ro-crate-metadata.json.

It needs detk, and R with the Bioconductor packages DESeq2 (which detk runs for the transform and the test), airway (the data) and org.Hs.eg.db (gene symbols). With conda, for example:

$ mamba create -n detk-r -c conda-forge -c bioconda \
    r-base r-jsonlite r-data.table bioconductor-deseq2 \
    bioconductor-airway bioconductor-org.hs.eg.db

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
airway (GEO GSE52778) is human airway smooth muscle cells from four donor cell lines, each treated with dexamethasone (trt) or left untreated (untrt): 8 samples, 63,677 Ensembl genes. It is Bioconductor's standard RNA-seq teaching dataset, so every result here can be checked against the DESeq2 vignette. The counts come from the airway Bioconductor data package, which redistributes the published gene counts (Himes et al. 2014, PMID 24926665).

detk reads plain delimited files, so the first step writes the package's data out as three: the counts, the sample information, and a map from each Ensembl gene ID to its Entrez ID and gene symbol (from org.Hs.eg.db). Save this R script as prepare_data.R and run it:

cat > prepare_data.R <<'EOF'
suppressMessages({
    library(airway)
    library(org.Hs.eg.db)
})
data(airway)

# gene counts: Ensembl gene IDs x 8 samples
counts <- as.data.frame(assay(airway))
counts <- cbind(gene = rownames(counts), counts)
write.csv(counts, "counts.csv", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)

# sample information: cell line and treatment
cd <- as.data.frame(colData(airway)[, c("cell", "dex")])
cd <- cbind(sample = rownames(cd), cd)
write.csv(cd, "sample_info.csv", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)

# Ensembl gene ID -> Entrez ID and gene symbol (the first, where several)
ens <- rownames(assay(airway))
entrez <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = ens, column = "ENTREZID",
                 keytype = "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")
symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = ens, column = "SYMBOL",
                 keytype = "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")
map <- data.frame(gene = ens, entrez = unname(entrez), symbol = unname(symbol))
write.csv(map, "gene_map.csv", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
EOF
Rscript prepare_data.R 2> /dev/null
cat sample_info.csv

sample,cell,dex
SRR1039508,N61311,untrt
SRR1039509,N61311,trt
SRR1039512,N052611,untrt
SRR1039513,N052611,trt
SRR1039516,N080611,untrt
SRR1039517,N080611,trt
SRR1039520,N061011,untrt
SRR1039521,N061011,trt

Each cell line has one treated and one untreated sample, so the samples are paired by cell line: the design below compares treated with untreated within each cell line.

docs.title: Look at the raw counts
docs.text:
detk-stats summary computes the matrix's size, each sample's distribution of counts, the zeros in each sample and each gene, each sample's entropy and a principal component analysis. --log works on log counts, and --color-col=dex colors the report's plots by treatment:

detk-stats summary --log --color-col=dex -o raw_summary_stats.csv counts.csv sample_info.csv
head -n 4 raw_summary_stats.csv

#basestats
stat,val
num_cols,8
num_rows,63677

In the report's PCA the samples already separate by treatment along one component and by cell line along another.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
Most of the 63,677 genes are not expressed in these cells. Keep the genes with a nonzero count in at least half the samples; the report records what the rule removed:

detk-filter 'nonzero(all) >= 0.5' -o counts_filtered.csv counts.csv
tail -n +2 counts_filtered.csv | wc -l

24706

docs.title: Normalize
docs.text:
detk-norm deseq2 divides each sample by its DESeq2 size factor, the median ratio of its counts to each gene's geometric mean across the samples (in Python: this step needs no R). --size-factors writes the factors to a file, a header line and then a sample and its factor on each line:

detk-norm deseq2 -o norm_counts.csv --size-factors=size_factors.tsv counts_filtered.csv
cat size_factors.tsv

sample  size_factor
SRR1039508  1.02364...
SRR1039509  0.89616...
SRR1039512  1.17948...
SRR1039513  0.67005...
SRR1039516  1.17767...
SRR1039517  1.39903...
SRR1039520  0.92077...
SRR1039521  0.94451...

These are the size factors DESeq2's own estimateSizeFactors finds for the same counts. The normalized counts are for looking at and for methods that take them; DESeq2's test below estimates the size factors itself, so it takes the raw filtered counts, not norm_counts.csv.

docs.title: Variance-stabilize
docs.text:
Count variance grows with the mean, which lets the most expressed genes dominate distances and plots. DESeq2's variance-stabilizing transform (VST) removes that dependence; the report shows the distributions before and after and the mean-variance trend:

detk-transform vst -o vst_counts.csv counts_filtered.csv

docs.title: Flag outliers
docs.text:
detk-outlier entropy computes each gene's entropy across the samples, which is low for a gene whose counts come mostly from one or a few samples, and flags the genes with an entropy below the percentile -p sets. Count the flagged genes:

detk-outlier entropy counts_filtered.csv -p 0.05 -o entropy_flags.csv
head -n 3 entropy_flags.csv
grep -c ',True$' entropy_flags.csv

gene,entropy,entropy_p0_05
ENSG00000000003,2.0222...,False
ENSG00000000419,2.0524...,False
13

The flags are for looking at, in the report's entropy plot: nothing below removes the flagged genes.

docs.title: Differential expression
docs.text:
detk-de deseq2 runs DESeq2 on the raw filtered counts with a design written in detk's formula mini-language: the cell line as a covariate, and the treatment with untrt as its reference level, so a positive fold change is higher with dexamethasone:

detk-de deseq2 -o deseq2_results.csv "counts ~ cell + dex[untrt]" counts_filtered.csv sample_info.csv
head -n 1 deseq2_results.csv | tr , '\n' | grep dex

dex__trt__log2FoldChange
dex__trt__lfcSE
dex__trt__stat
dex__trt__pvalue
dex__trt__padj

The results have a row per gene and, after its mean normalized count (baseMean), five columns for each term of the design: the treatment's are named dex__trt__*, and the cell__* columns hold the cell line terms. The adjusted p-values (padj) are Benjamini-Hochberg over every gene in the file, without the independent filtering DESeq2's results() adds by default.

docs.title: Gene symbols
docs.text:
Ensembl IDs are hard to read. detk-util annotate adds the symbol column of the map from the first step to the results, joining on the gene ID; a gene with no symbol gets an empty one, and the command warns how many had none:

detk-util annotate --map-to=symbol -o deseq2_results_symbols.csv deseq2_results.csv gene_map.csv

Now a short table of the treatment's results, gene, symbol, fold change and adjusted p-value, sorted by the adjusted p-value (the awk program finds the columns by name in the header), and its first ten genes:

awk -F, -v OFS=, '
  NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) col[$i] = i; next }
  { printf "%s,%s,%.3f,%.3g\n", $1, $col["symbol"],
      $col["dex__trt__log2FoldChange"], $col["dex__trt__padj"] }
' deseq2_results_symbols.csv | sort -t, -k4,4g > top_genes.csv
head -n 10 top_genes.csv

ENSG00000152583,SPARCL1,4.575,9.52e-133
ENSG00000165995,CACNB2,3.291,2.84e-131
ENSG00000101347,SAMHD1,3.767,8.28e-125
ENSG00000120129,DUSP1,2.948,1.27e-124
ENSG00000189221,MAOA,3.354,3.12e-119
ENSG00000211445,GPX3,3.730,8.99e-108
ENSG00000157214,STEAP2,1.977,3.34e-100
ENSG00000162614,NEXN,2.036,4.05e-97
ENSG00000125148,MT2A,2.211,7.55e-92
ENSG00000154734,ADAMTS1,2.346,4.57e-86

All ten are higher with dexamethasone. They are the genes Bioconductor's RNA-seq workflow finds at the top for this dataset with the same design; DUSP1 and the metallothionein MT2A are well known glucocorticoid-induced genes.

docs.title: The report and the crate
docs.text:
Every detk command above that has a report wrote its results into detk_report/ and rendered the report again, so the report is already up to date. detk-report generate renders it from what is in the directory:

detk-report generate
ls detk_report

detk_report.html
json

Open detk_report/detk_report.html in a browser: it is one self-contained file, with a section for each step. The differential expression section is a volcano and an MA plot with a menu of the design's terms: switch between the treatment (dex__trt) and the cell lines. Next to the report, in the working directory, detk wrote ro-crate-metadata.json, a Process Run Crate that describes each step's command, its parameters and the files it read and wrote. The steps it lists (the summary is listed as the six statistics it is made of):

grep -o '"name": "detk-[^"]* run"' ro-crate-metadata.json | sort -u

"name": "detk-de deseq2 run"
"name": "detk-filter run"
"name": "detk-norm deseq2 run"
"name": "detk-outlier entropy run"
"name": "detk-stats basestats run"
"name": "detk-stats coldist run"
"name": "detk-stats colzero run"
"name": "detk-stats entropy run"
"name": "detk-stats pca run"
"name": "detk-stats rowzero run"
"name": "detk-transform vst run"
"name": "detk-util annotate run"

docs.title: Optional: gene set enrichment
docs.text:
This step downloads a gene set file, so the page shows it but its test does not run it, and the published report does not have it. It needs the R package fgsea as well (bioconductor-fgsea).

WikiPathways publishes its human pathways (CC0) as a GMT file keyed by Entrez gene ID; download the current one from https://data.wikipathways.org/current/gmt/, the file named wikipathways-<date>-gmt-Homo_sapiens.gmt, as wikipathways.gmt. The results are keyed by Ensembl ID, so join the map's entrez column on first. Several Ensembl genes can map to one Entrez ID and fgsea refuses an ID that appears twice, so the join also keeps one row per Entrez ID (the first). It needs pandas, which detk depends on, so run it with the Python detk is installed in (the python3 on PATH may lack pandas when detk was installed with uv tool install or pipx):

$ DETK_PY="$(dirname "$(command -v detk-de)")/python3"
$ [ -x "$DETK_PY" ] || DETK_PY=python3
$ "$DETK_PY" - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
res = pd.read_csv("deseq2_results.csv")
gmap = pd.read_csv("gene_map.csv", dtype=str)
res = res.merge(gmap[["gene", "entrez"]], left_on=res.columns[0], right_on="gene", how="left")
res = res.dropna(subset=["entrez"]).drop_duplicates(subset=["entrez"])
res.to_csv("deseq2_results_entrez.csv", index=False)
PY

Then rank the genes by the treatment's fold change and test each pathway:

$ detk-enrich fgsea --filter-unannotated -i entrez -c 'dex__trt__log2FoldChange' \
    -o fgsea_results.csv wikipathways.gmt deseq2_results_entrez.csv

-c names the ranking column; without it detk would rank by the last numeric column, the treatment's adjusted p-value, which ranks by the wrong quantity and in the wrong direction. The Wald statistic dex__trt__stat is the other common choice. Run detk-report generate again to add the enrichment to the report.

docs.title: From quantifier outputs to a normalized matrix
docs.text: Most RNA-seq analyses start from a quantifier's output: one file per sample, from salmon, kallisto, htseq-count or featureCounts. This tutorial takes salmon's quant.sf files to a counts matrix, matches it to a sample sheet, normalizes it to counts per million (CPM) and transcripts per million (TPM), log-transforms it, summarizes it, and ends with detk's report and its provenance crate. It needs detk and nothing else: no R.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The data are simulated, so you can share and change them freely: salmon outputs for six samples of a small study, three ctrl and three treat, over 300 made-up transcripts, plus P1, a pilot library that was quantified with them but is not part of the study. The seeded script simulate.py wrote them and writes the same files byte for byte each time it runs. Make them in an empty directory with the script, or copy them from a checkout of detk's repository, where they sit next to it in docs/tutorials/data/quantifiers/:

$ python simulate.py .

Salmon writes each sample to a directory of its own, and the file in each is called quant.sf:

ls salmon
head -n 3 salmon/S1/quant.sf

P1
S1
S2
S3
S4
S5
S6
Name    Length  EffectiveLength TPM NumReads
TX00001.2   1216    1029.500    2320.779735 124.000
TX00002.1   1577    1390.500    3782.946882 273.000

NumReads is salmon's estimate of the reads from each transcript. It is not always a whole number, because salmon shares a read between the transcripts it could have come from.

docs.title: Gather the counts into one matrix
docs.text:
detk-util gather reads every quant.sf and writes one matrix, a row per transcript and a column per sample. It detects the format from the files' header and takes the NumReads column. The files are all called quant.sf, so each sample is named after its directory. Quote the pattern, and detk expands it, taking the files in natural order:

detk-util gather -o counts.csv 'salmon/*/quant.sf'
head -n 4 counts.csv

,P1,S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6
TX00001.2,105.420,124.000,106.000,319.000,147.000,93.000,130.412
TX00002.1,266.000,273.000,305.000,631.000,216.000,229.270,279.000
TX00003.1,572.707,546.000,365.096,924.000,332.000,442.000,429.000

The transcript IDs and the counts are kept as salmon wrote them, version suffix (.2) and all; gather does not round the counts or add transcripts up to genes. Every sample must list the same transcripts, or gather stops and names the differences (--on-mismatch fills or drops them instead).

docs.title: Match the counts to the sample sheet
docs.text:
The study's sample sheet has a row per sample and its condition. The pilot library, P1, is not in it:

cat samples.csv

sample,condition
S1,ctrl
S2,ctrl
S3,ctrl
S4,treat
S5,treat
S6,treat

detk-util tidy keeps the samples that are in both files, in the order of the counts columns, so the counts lose P1. -p writes the sample sheet of those samples too, with the same columns and header as samples.csv:

detk-util tidy -o counts_tidy.csv -p samples_tidy.csv counts.csv samples.csv
head -n 1 counts_tidy.csv
head -n 2 samples_tidy.csv

,S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6
sample,condition
S1,ctrl

The steps below use the two tidied files.

docs.title: Counts per million
docs.text:
detk-norm cpm divides each sample's counts by its total and multiplies by one million, so each sample's library size no longer matters:

detk-norm cpm -o cpm.csv counts_tidy.csv

Each column of cpm.csv now sums to one million. Add up S1's:

awk -F, 'NR > 1 { total += $2 } END { printf "%.3f\n", total }' cpm.csv

1000000.000

docs.title: Transcripts per million
docs.text:
CPM does not allow for length: a long transcript gives more reads than a short one at the same abundance. TPM divides each count by its transcript's length in kilobases first, then scales each sample to one million. detk-norm tpm takes the lengths from a file with a transcript's name and length on each line. Salmon's EffectiveLength, the length less the fragments that could not fit at its ends, is the one to use; take it from any sample's quant.sf (the column header is skipped as a header):

cut -f 1,3 salmon/S1/quant.sf > lengths.tsv
detk-norm tpm -o tpm.csv counts_tidy.csv lengths.tsv
head -n 2 tpm.csv

,S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6
TX00001.2,2320.7797353...,2052.8858193...,2599.2973373...,2121.6721760...,2000.4695925...,2651.0503475...

These are salmon's own TPM, which you saw in the first line of S1's quant.sf (2320.779735). In this simulated study every sample has the same effective lengths. In real data each sample's differ a little, with its fragment lengths, so detk's TPM from one sample's lengths is close to salmon's but not the same.

docs.title: Log-transform
docs.text:
Counts and their normalized values span orders of magnitude, so most plots and many methods work on their logarithm. detk-transform plog takes the log of each value plus a pseudocount, here log2(CPM + 1):

detk-transform plog -b 2 -o log2cpm.csv cpm.csv

docs.title: Summary statistics
docs.text:
detk-stats summary computes the matrix's size, the distribution of each sample's values, the zeros in each sample and each transcript, each sample's entropy and a principal component analysis. With the sample sheet it colors the report's plots by condition:

detk-stats summary --color-col=condition -o summary.csv log2cpm.csv samples_tidy.csv
head -n 4 summary.csv

#basestats
stat,val
num_cols,6
num_rows,300

docs.title: The report and the crate
docs.text:
Every detk command above that has a report wrote its results into detk_report/ and rendered the report again, so the report is already up to date. detk-report generate renders it from what is in the directory, for when you have removed or added module files by hand:

detk-report generate
ls detk_report

detk_report.html
json

Open detk_report/detk_report.html in a browser: it is one self-contained file, with a section for each step. Next to it, in the working directory, detk wrote ro-crate-metadata.json, a Process Run Crate that describes each step's command, its parameters and the files it read and wrote, in terms any RO-Crate tool can read. The steps it lists (the summary is listed as the six statistics it is made of):

grep -o '"name": "detk-[^"]* run"' ro-crate-metadata.json | sort -u

"name": "detk-norm cpm run"
"name": "detk-norm tpm run"
"name": "detk-stats basestats run"
"name": "detk-stats coldist run"
"name": "detk-stats colzero run"
"name": "detk-stats entropy run"
"name": "detk-stats pca run"
"name": "detk-stats rowzero run"
"name": "detk-transform plog run"
"name": "detk-util gather run"
"name": "detk-util tidy run"
